why_angle: The rival pages only list single EcoFlow bundles. They never total what a full 60 kWh build costs, never give a cost per Wh, and never compare EcoFlow against Anker with the needed home panel counted. This page adds up both builds part by part at today's store prices: 61.44 kWh for $26,691 bare, $29,691 with Smart Home Panel 3, or $29,092 for the E10 with Power Dock. It also shows why neither build reaches 60 kW.

page.title: Best Solar Generators for 60,000W: What 60 kW and 60 kWh Really Cost
page.h1: Best solar generators for 60000W: what 60 kW and 60 kWh systems cost
page.desc: No 120/240 V solar generator reaches 60,000 W. Here is what a 60 kWh EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra X or Anker SOLIX E10 build costs today, part by part.
page.answer: Short answer. No 120/240 V home solar generator reaches 60,000 W: the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra X has the highest maximum output, 36 kW from three units. For 60,000 Wh of battery capacity, one DELTA Pro Ultra X with 10 batteries holds 61.44 kWh for $26,691, or $0.43 per Wh.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra X, 61.44 kWh: $7,899 bundle (1 inverter + 2 batteries) + 8 × $2,349 extra batteries = $26,691; $26,691 ÷ 61,440 Wh = $0.43 per Wh.
  • The same build with a home panel: the Smart Control Kit (inverter + Smart Home Panel 3 with 32 circuits + 2 batteries) costs $10,899, and $10,899 + 8 × $2,349 = $29,691, or $0.48 per Wh. With the Smart Transfer Kit, which uses the 6-circuit Smart Gateway (200A): $9,799 + $18,792 = $28,591, or $0.47 per Wh.
  • Anker SOLIX E10, 61.44 kWh: $14,098 bundle (2 power modules + 4 batteries + Power Dock) + 6 × $2,499 = $29,092; $29,092 ÷ 61,440 Wh = $0.47 per Wh. Output is 2 × 7,680 W = 15.36 kW, against 12 kW for the single EcoFlow inverter.
  • Weight: EcoFlow 76.06 + 10 × 111.3 = 1,189 lb; Anker 2 × 60.6 + 10 × 130 = 1,421 lb, not counting the dock.
  • Runtime: 61,440 Wh ÷ 12,000 W = 5.1 hours at the EcoFlow's full output. At a 2,500 W average it is 61,440 ÷ 2,500 = 24.6 hours, before conversion losses.
  • Why 60 kW is out of reach: 60 kW ÷ 12 kW = 5 DELTA Pro Ultra X inverters, but EcoFlow allows 3 (36 kW). 60 kW ÷ 7.68 kW = 7.8 E10 units, but one Power Dock takes 3 (22.8 kW rated).

What a 60 kWh solar generator costs, part by part

Both home systems store energy in 6,144 Wh battery modules, so 10 modules make 61.44 kWh in each case. The difference is how many inverters you need to hold them. One DELTA Pro Ultra X inverter takes up to 10 batteries, so a single 12 kW inverter carries the whole 61.44 kWh. An E10 power module takes up to 5 B6000 batteries, so 60 kWh needs two modules and Anker's Power Dock to join them. That extra module costs more, but it also adds output: 15.36 kW rated, or 20 kW turbo for 90 minutes.

The EcoFlow price advantage depends on how you connect it to the house. Battery-only, the DELTA Pro Ultra X is $2,401 cheaper than the E10. Add the Smart Home Panel 3 kit and it costs $599 more than the E10, whose bundle already includes the Power Dock (200 A grid and subpanel connection, ≤20 ms switchover). EcoFlow says Smart Home Panel 3 requires installation, with a fee set after assessment. None of the prices here include installation. On battery life, Anker states 80% capacity after 4,000 cycles. EcoFlow's DELTA Pro Ultra X spec page gives no cycle figure.

We don't link to the DELTA Pro Ultra X; EcoFlow sells it from its US store. The E10 build is available here: {buy:anker-solix-e10-2-power-module-4-battery-power-dock}. Add six B6000 add-on batteries to reach 61.44 kWh. The original DELTA Pro Ultra (7.2–21.6 kW) shows as unavailable on EcoFlow's US store as of 2026-11-10.

If you truly need 60,000 W of continuous output, you need commercial equipment. The Sol-Ark 60K-3P-480V delivers 60,000 W, but only at 277/480 V three-phase, and the seller says it is designed for commercial and industrial customers. Both home systems above output 120/240 V split phase. The Sol-Ark also ships without batteries and needs a 300 V+ bank, so neither EcoFlow nor Anker batteries will work with it.

Not recommended

Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus for a 60 kWh goal. Anker lists it as expandable to 53.8 kWh at 12 kW, so it can't reach 60 kWh at all. The largest build is the two-unit Smart Home Power Kit plus 12 BP3800 batteries: $7,799.99 + 12 × $1,999.99 = $31,799.87. That works out to $31,799.87 ÷ 53,760 Wh = $0.59 per Wh, which costs more than either 61.44 kWh build above and stores less.

The page says '30-Day Money-Back Guarantee for Any Reason' and 'Undamaged products can be returned for a full refund, regardless of the reason, within 30 days of receipt'. It also requires all accessories and the original packaging, and the customer pays shipping on non-quality returns. The US store refund policy, https://us.ankersolix.com/policies/refund-policy, read 2026-11-10, gives the same 30-day window and requires batteries to be below 30% charge before return. Returns is a product-record field, not a figure on the page, so no page source was added.
The E10 product page at us.ankersolix.com returned HTTP 429 to both storecheck.py and WebFetch, so I could not read the returns text there. I did not re-check the $14,098 price.

Left unchanged because it was outside this fix: the E10 warranty page, read 2026-11-10, lists the Power Module at 5 years, the B6000 Battery at '5 Years or 15 MWh Throughput, Whichever Comes First' and the Power Dock at 10 years. The draft's 'warranty' value says only '5 years (power module and battery module)', so it leaves out the 15 MWh cap and the Power Dock's 10 years. The checks may want to flag this.
